Activation steering works by adding a vector to a model's residual stream at inference time to reliably shift behavior — suppress refusals, induce a persona, amplify a concept — and the central question here is what happens when you compose two or more such vectors targeting different behavioral dimensions simultaneously. The naive hope is linear superposition: steer toward "be concise" and "be formal" and get a response that is both. The expert worry is that this hope collapses in practice because instruction-tuned models have dense, entangled representations where "formal register" and "refusal suppression" may share basis components in the residual stream — so composing them doesn't add two clean effects but instead corrupts both, or produces a third emergent behavior neither vector was meant to induce. What a beginner misses is that "orthogonal in behavioral space" does not imply "orthogonal in activation space": two behaviors that seem semantically unrelated can have heavily overlapping geometric footprints in the layers where steering is applied, particularly in mid-to-late attention layers where polysemantic features are densest. The deeper expert concern is interference asymmetry — one vector may partially null out the other's effect while the second dominates, making composed steering unreliable in ways that are hard to predict without exhaustive empirical probing of each layer and each vector pair.

Anthropic's work on sparse autoencoders (the April 2024 "Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders" paper on Claude's internals) gives you a concrete tool: run the SAE on the post-intervention activations and compare which features light up versus the single-vector cases — emergent behavior should activate a distinct feature cluster, while dominance should look like one vector's feature set essentially reproducing intact. A behavioral complement is a factorial output probe: construct a 2x2 evaluation suite scoring outputs on dimension A alone and dimension B alone (e.g., refusal rate for one, formality classifier score for the other), then compare the composed-steering cell to the single-steering and no-steering cells — dominance shows one score preserved and one collapsed back to baseline, while mutual interference shows both degraded, and emergence shows neither score matching predictions from either vector independently. The numbers matter here: in Zou et al.'s 2023 "Representation Engineering" work, single steering vectors applied at layer 15–20 of a 40-layer model achieved ~85–95% behavioral shift rates; if your composed condition drops both target behaviors below 50%, that's a strong interference signature rather than dominance. What most practitioners miss is that you need this diagnosis per layer, not just globally — a pair might destructively interfere at layer 16 but show clean superposition at layer 22, meaning layer choice is a confound you must control before drawing any conclusion about the vector pair's inherent composability.

The difference-in-means (DiM) vector is essentially a prompted direction — it captures the mean activation shift your specific contrastive pairs induce, which conflates the true behavioral dimension with whatever stylistic, topical, or demographic correlates your prompts happen to share. Switching to PCA-derived vectors (taking the top PC of activation variance across a broader, more diverse prompt set) tends to produce directions that are more geometrically "clean" in the sense of explaining more variance with less prompt-distribution leakage — Marks & Tegmark's 2023 "The Geometry of Truth" paper showed that for factual recall, the top PC of activations across diverse prompts aligned more robustly with the truth direction than DiM vectors derived from narrow prompt sets, suggesting PCA partially deconfounds the extraction. If you then rerun your interference experiment with PCA vectors, reduced interference would implicate your original DiM construction as the culprit — the vectors were interfering partly because both were contaminated by shared prompt-distribution artifacts (e.g., both "refusal" and "formality" DiM vectors extracted from GPT-4-class models might both partially encode "assistant-style hedging language" simply because your prompts elicited it). Conversely, if interference persists or worsens with PCA vectors, that's strong evidence the entanglement is structural — baked into how the model's weights represent those dimensions, not an artifact of your extraction method. The most telling experiment is to compare the cosine similarity between your DiM and PCA vectors for each behavioral dimension: high similarity (>0.85, roughly) means extraction method probably doesn't explain the interference; low similarity means you've been steering a confounded direction all along. This framing reframes the whole question productively — interference patterns are a joint property of the model's representational geometry and your measurement apparatus, and you cannot attribute them to either alone without this kind of extraction-method ablation.

The cleanest discriminator is a surgical ablation probe: train a linear classifier to predict behavior A from residual stream activations, then project out that direction from the activations and measure how much performance on task B degrades — if removing the A-direction causes substantial B-degradation (say, >15% on a held-out behavioral benchmark), that's evidence of functional dependency, not just training co-occurrence. The worrying case — which gets underappreciated — is when entanglement survives both ablation and fine-tuning, suggesting the model has learned a genuine computational dependency: perhaps "formal register" and "deferential compliance" are entangled because the instruction-tuning process reinforced them together so consistently that the model now uses one as a heuristic signal for the other during generation, making clean separation actively harmful to coherent behavior.
